title: 情報戦に負けた戦後日本　高市首相、インテリジェンス強化への条件
extracted_text:
高市早苗政権はインテリジェンス（情報収集・分析）能力を高めることを目指し、「スパイ防止法」の制定を視野に入れる。戦後の日本が外国からの政治工作に無防備だったことを受けた改革といえる。その原因は組織や法律がなかったからなのだろうか。

ドイツ連邦公文書館に毛筆でしたためた一通の手紙が眠る。「友好の輪をより大きくするためにも閣下が一日も早くわが国を訪問されますことを望む次第です」。差出人は自民党の佐藤一郎衆院議員。大蔵官僚出身で経済企画庁長官などの要職を務めた政治家だ。

1984年6月、事務所の封筒に入れ、共産圏の中核国家だった東独の国家指導層のミッターク政治局員に送った。

3カ月後、重ねて書簡を送る。「閣下の訪日は必ずや両国の相互友好発展に多大な貢献をなすものと確信」と誘った。外務省も東独政府に「いまが好機」と伝え、訪日を促した。

日本が東独との通商拡大に前のめりだ――。そう判断したミッターク氏はすぐには動かず、少しじらして86年に東独の政府専用機で堂々と日本に降り立つ。

表向きは友好親善を装ったが、随行員には腹心の謀略家、シャルク・ゴロトコフスキ貿易次官を選んだ。ソ連国家保安委員会（KGB）に直結する情報機関、国家保安省の大佐で、産業スパイの統括役である。

スパイを自ら呼び込んでしまった日本。結末は明らかだった。東独は経済官僚や大使館員を総動員し、ハイテク企業に接触した。東芝などが東独の半導体量産に協力することを決めた。

ミッターク氏は帰国後、報告書に誇らしげに書き込んだ。「交渉の結果、何社かの日本企業は禁輸品を渡すことに同意した」。独裁国家の真の姿を直視せず、交流に取り組む政治家を利用した。

東独と関係をもったのは佐藤氏だけではない。檜垣徳太郎、鍋島直紹、河野謙三、桜内義雄の各氏。東独の機密文書には自民党議員が多く登場する。なかには結果的に対日工作の便宜につながったような記録もある。商談を仲介するような例もみられた。

日本政府も認識が甘かった。「日本の半導体製造装置が東南アジア経由で東独に流れている」。米国は水面下で日本に警告した。外務省は「不審な点はない」と素通りしていた。

なぜ「スパイ天国」を許してしまったのか。自民党も政府も財界も危機感がなかったのが最大の問題ではないか。日本は「不都合な事実」や「負の過去」を直視するのが苦手だ。

いまも日本はロシアでの資源ビジネスにこだわる。デュアルユース（軍民両用）の日本製品は東南アジアなどを通じてロシアに流れている。サプライチェーン（供給網）には中国が深く組み込まれている。それを注視する欧米の情報機関を取材すると、冷戦時代と変わらぬ日本の「危機感の欠如」や「事なかれ主義」を憂える声が聞こえる。

日本が再び情報戦で負けないようにインテリジェンス機能は高めた方がいい。それは政府・与党を守るのではなく民主主義を守るツールでなくてはならない。

東京大学の井形彬特任講師はインテリジェンス改革を「緊急課題」としつつ、独立した第三者機関や裁判所による承認などで乱用を防ぐ仕組みが大切だとクギを刺す。不服申立制度なども必要だという。

将来の開示を前提に活動記録を文書で残すことや国会による民主的統制も考慮すべきだろう。なにより国民に丁寧に説明し、社会全体で危機感を共有することが不可欠だ。それが高市政権の優先課題ではないか。

（欧州駐在編集委員　赤川省吾）

translated_text:
The Takachi administration aims to strengthen intelligence (information gathering and analysis) capabilities, considering the enactment of an Anti-espionage Law. This reform comes in response to Japan's lack of defense against foreign political operations in the postwar period. Was the reason simply the absence of organizations and laws?

A letter handwritten in brush script lies dormant in the German Federal Archives. "I sincerely hope that Your Excellency will visit our country at the earliest possible opportunity to expand the circle of friendship." The sender was Ichiro Sato, a member of the House of Representatives from the Liberal Democratic Party. A former Treasury official, he served in key positions such as Director of the Economic Planning Agency.

In June 1984, it was sent in an envelope to his office, addressed to Politburo member Mittaerk of East Germany, the core nation of the Communist bloc.

Three months later, another letter followed. "I am confident that Your Excellency's visit will surely greatly contribute to the mutual friendly development of both countries," it read, extending the invitation. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs also conveyed to the East German government that "now is the best time" and urged the visit.

Japan was eager to expand trade with East Germany—Mittak determined. He did not act immediately but waited, arriving in Japan on an official East German aircraft in 1986.

Outwardly posing as a mission of friendship, he chose as his accompanying staff a trusted schemer, Deputy Trade Minister Shargu Gorotokov. A colonel in the State Security Ministry, an intelligence agency directly connected to the KGB, he was the coordinator of industrial espionage.

Japan had invited the spy in himself. The outcome was clear. East Germany mobilized its economic officials and embassy staff to make contact with high-tech companies. Toshiba and others agreed to assist in semiconductor mass production in East Germany.

After returning home, Mittaerk proudly wrote in his report: "As a result of negotiations, several Japanese companies agreed to provide prohibited items." He had used politicians engaged in exchange without confronting the true nature of the dictatorial state.

Sato was not the only one to develop ties with East Germany. Others included Tokutarou Higashida, Naotsugu Nabeshima, Kenzo Kono, and Yoshio Sakurauchi. Many Liberal Democratic Party politicians appear in East German classified documents. Some records even facilitated anti-Japan intelligence operations. Certain politicians are seen as having acted as intermediaries in commercial negotiations.

The Japanese government also showed naive understanding. "Japanese semiconductor manufacturing equipment is flowing to East Germany via Southeast Asia." The US secretly warned Japan, but the Foreign Ministry dismissed it as "nothing suspicious."

Why did Japan allow itself to become a "spy haven"? The lack of crisis awareness among the LDP, government, and business community was the biggest problem. Japan struggles to face "inconvenient facts" and "negative past."

Japan continues to pursue resource business in Russia. Dual-use Japanese products are flowing to Russia via Southeast Asia. Supply chains are deeply integrated with China. When interviewed, Western intelligence agencies monitoring these flows express concern about Japan's continuing "lack of crisis awareness" and "risk-averse attitude" from the Cold War era.

It would be better to strengthen intelligence functions so Japan does not lose in another information war. This is not about protecting the government or ruling party—it must be a tool for safeguarding democracy.

Tokyo University Special Lecturer Akira Igata emphasizes intelligence reform as "an urgent issue," while stressing the importance of mechanisms to prevent abuse through independent third-party or court authorization. An appeals system would also be necessary.

Activities should be documented with future disclosure in mind, and democratic control by the National Diet should be considered. Ultimately, carefully explaining to citizens and building shared crisis awareness throughout society is essential. Isn't this a priority for the Takachi administration?

(European Correspondent Seigo Akagawa)
title_en: Postwar Japan Lost in Information Warfare: PM Takachi, Conditions for Strengthening Intelligence
